newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - China in Australian iron project talks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - China in Australian iron project talks.

text.p: Australian United Steel Industry Ltd (AUSI) is holding talks with China about it buying a stake of about 20 percent in AUSI's A$1.9 billion direct reduced iron (DRI) project planned for Western Australia, project chairman Sir Russel Madigan said on Tuesday.
The talks were being held with China's state-owned Ministry of Metallurgical Industries and its investment arm, he said.
This group is the vehicle for China's joint venture stake, with the RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd group, in the existing Channar iron ore mine in Western Australia.

"I used that analogy with them, having been the chairman of (RTZ-CRA unit) Hamersley when they did that. I said 'that's been a great success'. They said 'yes'. I said 'well, here's another one'," Madigan said in an interview.

While China's potential dollar-value investment in the DRI plant could not be stated at present, it was hoped China would take about one-third of the project's production about four million tonnes of DRI a year, Madigan said.
AUSI was talking with other potential investors, he said.
The team from the Chinese ministry and its investment arm in Channar would soon leave for Mexico and Argentina, to examine applications of DRI, Madigan said.

Howard's promotion of the concept of Chinese joint-venture processing of iron ore in Western Australia was very logical given the state's resources of ore and natural gas as well as its proximity to the China market, he said.
The Chinese could be interested in other projects in the state as well as in the AUSI project, planned for Cape Lambert in the Pilbara iron ore province, he said.
AUSI was talking with many potential financiers, including the Chinese. Negotiations were confidential, he said.
Madigan also said shareholdings in AUSI changed frequently because groups were paid for work in shares, not cash.

Interests in the project included Madigan, former CRA chief Sir Roderick Carnegie, former Australian Ambassador to China Ross Garnaut, as well as Kaiser Engineers Pty Ltd, Macquarie Bank Ltd, Norwegian-based international engineering group Kvaerner ASA, Mobil Corp subsidiary Ampolex Ltd, German steelmaker Georgsmarienhutte and others.
"It's a very eclectic group of shareholders," Madigan said.
Madigan was speaking after returning from a recent trip to China in a delegation led by Australian Prime Minister John Howard, a mission he rated as "very helpful".

Chinese premier Li Peng agreed during a meeting with Howard to send a feasibility study mission to examine the AUSI DRI plant proposal and possibly other iron ore processing plants proposed for Western Australia. Howard also raised the ore processing issue with China's vice-premier Zhu Rongji.
"I think it will bear fruit," Madigan said.
The Chinese government's "chop" (stamp) on the assessment visit to Australia might open interest beyond the AUSI venture, he said.
AUSI had virtually completed its feasibility study and conceptually the project was now mature.
It had completed its figures, preliminary designs, siting, access arrangements and ore supply contract and was negotiating for gas supplies, Madigan also said.
The focus was now on finance, he said.
Acquisition by a project customer of a large stake in the venture would help with bank financing, Madigan said.
AUSI, hoping for finance early next year for start-up in 2000, last month signed an agreement with Hamersley Iron to take 7.5 million tonnes of iron fines a year.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
